title: Map of volcanoes and earthquakes: Ring of Fire
subject: Earth & space

sources.title: NGSS 4-ESS2-2: Analyze and interpret data from maps to describe patterns of Earth's features
National Geographic Education: Ring of Fire

steps.title: Continents
steps.instruction: Trace the four continents around the big ocean.

note.text: This simplified map shows the lands around the Pacific Ocean: Asia and Australia on one side, the Americas on the other.

steps.title: Ring of Fire
steps.instruction: Trace the curved line around the edge of the ocean.

note.text: This horseshoe-shaped path is the Ring of Fire. About 90 percent of Earth's earthquakes happen along it.
note.remember: Ring of Fire: around the Pacific.

steps.title: Volcanoes
steps.instruction: Trace the seven volcanoes along the ring.

note.text: About three out of every four of Earth's volcanoes, more than 450, are on the Ring of Fire.
note.remember: Most volcanoes are on the ring.

steps.title: Find the pattern
steps.question: What pattern does the map show about where volcanoes are?

options.text: Many are in a ring around the edge of the Pacific Ocean
options.feedback: Yes. Volcanoes and earthquakes aren't scattered randomly: they line up around the Pacific.
Look again: they cluster in a line around the ocean's edge.

options.text: They're all in the middle of the ocean
options.feedback: On this map they follow the edges of the ocean, near the coasts.
There is one: they follow a ring around the Pacific.

steps.title: Why there?
steps.question: Earth's surface is broken into giant pieces called plates. Why are so many volcanoes and earthquakes on the Ring of Fire?

options.text: The ring follows the edges where plates meet
options.feedback: Right. The Ring of Fire traces the boundaries between several plates, where the ground is most active.

options.text: The ocean water heats the rocks
options.feedback: The cause is underground: the ring follows the edges of Earth's plates.
People don't cause volcanoes. The ring follows plate edges.

options.text: It's the hottest part of Earth
options.feedback: It's not about air temperature. The ring follows where plates meet.
